sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- lsp_diagnostics: Get diagnostics from configured LSP servers selected by file extension
- lsp_fix: Apply configured LSP source fixes to a file
- codemode: Run JavaScript that calls other tools

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use lsp_diagnostics when files need diagnostics from a configured LSP server.
- Use the server parameter only when the user asks for a specific configured LSP server or multiple servers match the same extension.
- If a configured server command is missing, report the configuration error and suggest installing it or updating the server's command in pi-lsp.json.
- Use lsp_fix for files handled by a configured LSP code-action server.
- Use kind when the server needs a specific source action kind such as source.organizeImports.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description:
Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

Codemode: `tools.read(args)` resolves to `string | { data: string; mimeType: string; note: string; type: "image"; }`.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description:
Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

Codemode: `tools.bash(args)` resolves to `{ output, truncated, full_output_path?, exit_code, wall_time_seconds }`.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description:
Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

Codemode: `tools.edit(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description:
Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

Codemode: `tools.write(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: lsp_diagnostics
toolsAdded.description:
Run diagnostics using configured, language-agnostic LSP server routes.

Codemode: `tools.lsp_diagnostics(args)` resolves to a string.

paths.description: Files or directories to check. Defaults to the workspace root and routes by configured server extensions.

root.description: Workspace root for language servers. Defaults to cwd.

limit.description: Maximum files to open per selected server.

server.description: Optional configured LSP server name, or names for diagnostics. Defaults to all servers matching the file extension.

toolsAdded.name: lsp_fix
toolsAdded.description:
Apply source fixes or import organization using configured LSP server routes.

Codemode: `tools.lsp_fix(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: File to process. The server is selected from configured file extensions.

root.description: Workspace root for language servers. Defaults to cwd.

write.description: Write changed text back to the file. Defaults to false.

server.description: Optional configured LSP server name. Defaults to extension-based inference.

kind.description: Source action kind. Defaults to source.fixAll.

toolsAdded.name: codemode
toolsAdded.description:
Run JavaScript that calls other tools. The input is raw JavaScript (not JSON, no code fence), run as an async function body in a QuickJS sandbox: top-level `await` and `return` work. No Node, file system, network, or timers.
- `await tools.<name>({ ...args })` resolves to a string, or an object if the tool's declaration says so, and rejects with an Error on failure. A tool whose declaration returns an object resolves on failure too when it returned that object; check its fields. Calls still running when the script ends are cancelled.
- Optional first line: `// @options: {"max_output_tokens": 10000, "timeout_ms": 60000}`

Globals:
- `text(value)`, `image(dataUrlOrImageBlock)`, `console.log(...)`, and top-level `return` add output; `exit()` ends the script. With several text items, each starts with a `==> text N/M <==` line, and `console` lines follow the other output in one `<console_output>` block. `image()` also saves the image to a temp file and the result names its path.
- `store(key, value)` and `load(key)` keep JSON values across codemode calls.
- `ALL_TOOLS`, `await searchTools(query, { limit?, namespace? })`, `await describeTool(name)`, `await describeNamespace(name)`: find unlisted tools, such as MCP tools.
- `models`: classifiers and image generation. Read /usr/lib/node_modules/pi/packages/coding-agent/docs/codemode.md first.

content.text: Write a Julia macro `@memoize` for function definitions (`function f(args...) ... end` and `f(x) = ...`) that caches results by argument tuple. Recursive calls must hit the cache. The cache should be typed from the argument annotations when they are concrete, so lookups don't box. Show `fib(90)` and state the macro's limitations.

content.thinking:
The user wants a Julia macro `@memoize` that:
1. Works with both `function f(args...) ... end` and `f(x) = ...` syntaxes
2. Caches results by argument tuple
3. Recursive calls must hit the cache
4. Cache is typed from argument annotations when concrete (avoid boxing)
5. Show `fib(90)` result
6. State the macro's limitations

Let me think about the design:

- For typed dispatch without boxing: if arguments have concrete type annotations (e.g., `x::Int`, `y::Float64`), we should generate a method with that concrete type, or use `typeof(x)` dispatch.
- For recursion: the function body needs to be able to call itself via the memoized dispatch, so we need to define the method *before* the function body is entered.
- For `function f(args...) ... end`: we need to rewrite this into a dispatch method definition.
- For `f(x) = expr`: this is a one-line assignment, we convert it to a `@generated` method or a typed method.

Key challenge: for `function f(args...) ... end`, we need to:
1. Generate a method signature with concrete types (if annotations exist)
2. Insert a memoization layer (e.g., a `get!` on a dictionary) before the body
3. The function body can call `f` recursively, and since the outer dispatch was already generated, recursive calls will go through the memoized method

Actually, the cleanest approach:
- For `function f(args...) ... end`: Generate a method `f(args::ConcreteTypes...)` that checks the cache, and if miss, calls `f(args...)` (the untyped version) to compute and store. Wait, but then recursive calls within the body would still go through the memoized version.

Actually, better approach:
- Generate the memoized method first (with concrete types), then define the original function. The memoized method checks the cache, and if miss, calls the original function. Since recursive calls use the untyped `f(args...)`, they go through the memoized dispatch (because Julia's method dispatch will pick the most specific one).

Wait, actually: if the memoized method has concrete types (e.g., `f(x::Int, y::Int)`), and the function body calls `f(x, y)`, Julia will dispatch to the memoized method (it's more specific than `f(args...)`). So recursive calls will hit the cache. Good.

But there's a subtlety: we need the memoized method to be defined *before* the function body is compiled, so that recursive calls within the body can dispatch to it. We can do this with `@eval` or by generating the code in the right order.

For the typed cache: use a `Dict{Tuple{types...}, result_type}` or `get!` with a closure. Actually, using `get!` with a closure is the idiomatic way.

Let me write this out:

```julia
macro memoize(expr)
    if expr.head == :function
        # function f(args...) ... end
        func_name = expr.args[2].args[1]
        arg_exprs = expr.args[2].args[2:end]  # (args, ...) tuple
        
        # Build type tuple from annotations
        arg_names = Expr[]
        arg_types = Type[]
        for arg in arg_exprs
            if arg.head == :(::)
                push!(arg_names, arg.args[1])
                push!(arg_types, arg.args[2])
            else
                push!(arg_names, arg)
                push!(arg_types, Any)  # untyped
            end
        end
        
        # Build cache key type and method signature
        if all(t -> t !== Any, arg_types)
            cache_type = :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)})
            method_args = [:(a$(i)::$(arg_types[i]) for i in 1:length(arg_types))]
        else
            cache_type = :(Tuple{Any})
            method_args = [:(a$(i) for i in 1:length(arg_types))]
        end
        
        # Generate: define memoized method first, then original function
        esc(quote
            $(method_args...) = ...  # memoized wrapper
            $expr  # original function
        end)
    elseif expr.head == :(=) && expr.args[1].head == :call
        # f(x) = expr
        func_name = expr.args[1].args[1]
        arg_name = expr.args[1].args[2]
        body = expr.args[2]
        # ...
    else
        error("@memoize only works with function definitions")
    end
end
```

Actually, let me think more carefully about the implementation. The key insight is:

1. Define a memoized dispatch method with concrete types
2. The original function (or the fallback) computes and stores in the cache
3. Recursive calls go through the memoized method

For the typed cache, I'll use `get!` with a closure that stores the result:

```julia
@eval function $(name)($(arg_names)...::$(concrete_types)...)
    _memo_cache = $(esc(quote
        @memoize_cache($(name), $(arg_types), $(quote($(arg_types[1])...$(arg_types[n])...))) end))
    # ...
end
```

Actually, the cleanest way is to define a per-function cache at module level, keyed by the concrete tuple type:

```julia
@memoize_cache(name, types) = get!(name => Dict{Tuple{types...}, Any}(), @__MODULE__(), :memoize_cache)
```

Then the generated code:
```julia
function f(a::Int, b::Int)
    cache = get!(@__MODULE__(), :memoize_cache_f, Dict{Tuple{Int,Int},Any})
    key = (a, b)
    if haskey(cache, key)
        return cache[key]
    end
    result = f(a, b)  # This would be infinite recursion!
    cache[key] = result
    return result
end
```

Wait, that's wrong - calling `f(a, b)` from within `f(a::Int, b::Int)` would dispatch to the same method. We need to either:
- Have the body call an internal version (e.g., `f_`), or
- Use a different approach

The standard pattern is:
```julia
function f(a::Int, b::Int)
    cache = get!(@__MODULE__(), :memoize_cache_f, Dict{Tuple{Int,Int},Any})
    key = (a, b)
    if haskey(cache, key)
        return cache[key]
    end
    result = _f(a, b)  # internal non-memoized version
    cache[key] = result
    return result
end

_f(a::Int, b::Int) = ...  # actual body
```

Or, define the memoized method first, then the body function, and have the memoized method call the body function.

Actually the cleanest pattern:

```julia
# Generated:
const _memo_f = @memoize_cache(f, Int, Int)

function f(a::Int, b::Int)
    if haskey(_memo_f, (a,b))
        return _memo_f[(a,b)]
    end
    result = f_body(a, b)
    _memo_f[(a,b)] = result
    return result
end

f_body(a::Int, b::Int) = ...  # the actual computation
```

This way:
- The memoized method has concrete types → no boxing
- Recursive calls `f(a, b)` dispatch to the memoized method (concrete type is more specific)
- The cache is keyed by `Tuple{Int, Int}`

For untyped args, we fall back to `Tuple{Any}` (boxes everything) but it's the best we can do.

Let me write the actual macro now. I need to handle:
- `function f(args...) ... end` with optional type annotations
- `f(x) = expr` (one-liner)
- For the one-liner, I need to handle the case where `x` has a type annotation: `f(x::Int) = expr`

Let me code this up properly.

For the `@memoize` macro:

```julia
macro memoize(expr)
    @assert expr.head == :function || expr.head == :(=) "@memoize expects function or f(x)=expr"
    
    if expr.head == :function
        # function f(args...) ... end
        head = expr.args[2]  # (name, args, body)
        name = head.args[1]
        args = head.args[2]  # tuple of args
        body = expr.args[3]
        
        arg_names = Symbol[]
        arg_types = Expr[]
        for arg in args
            if arg.head == :(::)
                push!(arg_names, arg.args[1])
                push!(arg_types, arg.args[2])
            else
                push!(arg_names, arg)
                push!(arg_types, :Any)
            end
        end
        
        all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
        cache_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})
        
        # Generate cache name
        cache_name = esc(quote
            @memoize_cache($(esc(name)), $(arg_types...)) end)
        
        # Generate the memoized dispatch
        memoized = quote
            $(esc(quote
                function $(esc(name))($(map(n -> :($(n)::$(t)), arg_names)...))
                    cache = $(esc(cache_name))
                    key = ($(arg_names...),)
                    if haskey(cache, key)
                        return cache[key]
                    end
                    result = $(esc(name))_body($(arg_names...))
                    cache[key] = result
                    return result
                end
                
                $(esc(name))_body($(arg_names...)) = $(esc(body)) end))
        end
        
        # ...
    end
end
```

Hmm, this is getting complex. Let me think about it differently.

The simplest correct approach:

1. For `function f(args...) ... end`:
   - Generate a `const _memo_cache_f = @memoize_cache(f, ...)` at module level
   - Generate a new method `f(args::ConcreteTypes...)` that checks the cache and calls `_f(args...)`
   - Generate `_f(args...)` with the original body
   - The memoized method is more specific, so recursive `f(args...)` calls go through it

2. For `f(x) = expr`:
   - Same pattern but with one argument

Let me write this cleanly now.

Actually, I realize there's a subtlety with the one-liner form. `f(x) = expr` could be:
- `f(x) = x + 1` — single arg
- `f(x, y) = x + y` — multiple args  
- `f(x::Int) = x + 1` — single arg with annotation
- `f(x::Int, y::Float64) = x + y` — multiple with annotations

For the macro, I need to handle the parsed form. In Julia, `f(x) = expr` parses as `:(=)(f(x), expr)` where the LHS is a `call` node: `:(f(x))`.

Let me write the macro now. I'll create a file and test it.

Let me write a clean implementation:

```julia
macro memoize(expr)
    _memoize_func(expr)
end

function _memoize_func(expr)
    @assert expr.head == :function || expr.head == :(=)
    
    name, args, body, arg_types = if expr.head == :function
        head = expr.args[2]  # (name, args, body)
        name = head.args[1]
        args = head.args[2]
        body = expr.args[3]
        _extract_arg_types(args)
    else
        # :(f(args) = body)
        call = expr.args[1]  # :(f(args))
        name = call.args[1]
        args = call.args[2:end]  # tuple of args
        body = expr.args[2]
        _extract_arg_types(args)
    end
    
    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
    cache_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})
    
    # Cache variable name: unique per function
    cache_var = gensym("memo_cache")
    
    # The memoized method (concrete types, no boxing)
    memoized_args = all_concrete ? 
        [:(a$(i)::$(arg_types[i])) for i in 1:length(args)] :
        [:(a$(i)) for i in 1:length(args)]
    
    esc(quote
        local $cache_var = Dict{$cache_type, Any}()
        
        function $(esc(name))($(memoized_args...))
            key = ($(map(n -> esc(n), args)...),)
            if haskey($cache_var, key)
                return $cache_var[key]
            end
            result = $(esc(name))_body($(map(n -> esc(n), args)...))
            $cache_var[key] = result
            return result
        end
        
        $(esc(name))_body($(map(n -> esc(n), args)...)) = $(esc(body))
    end)
end

function _extract_arg_types(args)
    names = Symbol[]
    types = Expr[]
    for arg in args
        if arg.head == :(::)
            push!(names, arg.args[1])
            push!(types, arg.args[2])
        else
            push!(names, arg)
            push!(types, :Any)
        end
    end
    return names, types
end
```

Wait, there's an issue. When the macro generates `function f(a1, a2) ... end`, the recursive call `f(a1, a2)` inside the body will dispatch to `f(a1, a2)` which is the memoized version. But the memoized version calls `f_body(a1, a2)`, which is NOT memoized. That's correct for the top-level call.

But what about recursive calls *within* `f_body`? If `f_body` calls `f(x, y)`, that will dispatch to the memoized method (because `a1::Int` is more specific than `a1` for type `Int`). So recursive calls will hit the cache. 

However, there's a problem with the approach above: `f_body` has no type annotations, so it's `f_body(a1, a2)` where `a1` and `a2` are `Any`. When `f_body` calls `f(x, y)`, Julia needs to figure out which `f` to dispatch to. Since `f(a1::Int, a2::Int)` is more specific than `f(a1, a2)`, it will pick the memoized one. Good.

But wait - what if the original function has no type annotations at all? Then `all_concrete = false` and we use `Tuple{Any}`. That boxes everything. But there's no way around that without knowing the concrete types.

What about `function f(x) ... end` without annotations? We should still generate a memoized method but with `Tuple{Any}` key. That's the best we can do.

Actually, I realize there's another issue: the `cache_var = Dict{...}()` is inside the `quote` block but not inside a function. It needs to be at module scope. Let me use `@__MODULE__` to store the cache:

```julia
esc(quote
    local $cache_var = get!(getfield(@__MODULE__(), :memoize_cache), ... )
```

Hmm, that's getting complex. Simpler approach: use a module-level `const` with a unique name:

```julia
esc(quote
    const $(esc(gensym("memo_cache_"))) = Dict{$cache_type, Any}()
    
    function $(esc(name))($(memoized_args...))
        cache = $(esc(gensym("memo_cache_")))
        ...
    end
end)
```

Actually, even simpler - just define the cache inside the macro's output at the top level of the generated code. Since `@memoize` is a macro that expands to module-level code, we can do:

```julia
esc(quote
    const _memo_cache_$(esc(name)) = Dict{$cache_type, Any}()
    
    function $(esc(name))($(memoized_args...))
        cache = _memo_cache_$(esc(name))
        key = ($(args...),)
        ...
    end
end)
```

But the `args` names are `a1`, `a2` etc (generated with `gensym`), not the original names. That's fine since the macro generates the whole function.

Wait, I used `a$(i)` with `gensym` for the memoized args. But the original `args` names are `Symbol[]` from `_extract_arg_types`. Let me use those:

Actually, the issue is: in `_extract_arg_types`, I extract the names but then in the macro expansion, I use `a$(i)`. The original names are in `names` array. Let me use those names.

But wait - what if the user writes `function f(x, y) ... end`? The original names are `:x`, `:y`. I should use those. The memoized method uses the same names with concrete type annotations.

Let me restructure:

```julia
macro memoize(expr)
    name, arg_names, arg_types, body = _parse(expr)
    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
    
    esc(quote
        const $(esc(gensym("cache_" * String(name)))) = Dict{
            $(all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})),
            Any
        }()
        
        function $(esc(name))($(map(i -> :($(esc(arg_names[i]))::$(arg_types[i])), 1:length(arg_names))...))
            cache = $(esc(gensym("cache_" * String(name))))
            key = ($(arg_names...),)
            if haskey(cache, key)
                return cache[key]
            end
            result = $(esc(name))_body($(arg_names...))
            cache[key] = result
            return result
        end
        
        $(esc(name))_body($(map(n -> :($(esc(n)))), arg_names...)) = $(esc(body))
    end)
end
```

Hmm, I need to be careful with escaping. The `arg_types` are `Expr`s (not symbols), so I need to `esc` them or they're already unevaluated since they're part of the expression. Actually, `arg_types` contains the AST nodes from the original expression, so they're already unevaluated. I can use them directly without `esc`.

Let me also handle the case where `arg_types[i]` is `:Any` - for untyped args, the generated method should be `function f(x) ...` (no annotation), and the cache key type is `Tuple{Any}`.

Actually wait, there's a subtle issue. If `arg_types[i]` is `:Any`, I shouldn't generate `x::Any` (that would make the method less specific, not more). Instead, I should just generate `x` (no annotation) and use `Tuple{Any}` as the cache type. But then the method signature is `f(x)` with `x::Any` implicit, and the cache is `Dict{Tuple{Any}, Any}`.

For the untyped case, the generated code would be:
```julia
const _memo_cache_f = Dict{Tuple{Any}, Any}()

function f(x)
    cache = _memo_cache_f
    key = (x,)
    if haskey(cache, key)
        return cache[key]
    end
    result = f_body(x)
    cache[key] = result
    return result
end

f_body(x) = x + 1
```

This works but boxes `x`. There's nothing we can do about that without knowing the concrete type.

For the typed case:
```julia
const _memo_cache_fib = Dict{Tuple{Int}, Int}()

function fib(x::Int)
    cache = _memo_cache_fib
    key = (x,)
    if haskey(cache, key)
        return cache[key]
    end
    result = fib_body(x)
    cache[key] = result
    return result
end

fib_body(x::Int) = x == 0 ? 0 : x + fib_body(x - 1)
```

Wait, `fib_body(x::Int)` should also have the type annotation for proper dispatch. Actually it doesn't need it since `fib_body` is only called from the memoized method with known types. But for safety and clarity, I'll add it.

Now, for the recursive fib(90):
```julia
@memoize
function fib(n::Int)::Int
    n <= 1 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
```

"""
@memoize macro for Julia function definitions.

Usage:
    @memoize
    function f(x::Int)::Int
        x == 0 ? 0 : x * f(x - 1)
    end

    @memoize g(x::Float64) = x + 1   # one-liner form also works

Caches results by argument tuple. Recursive calls dispatch through the
memoized method (concrete-type method is more specific than the untyped
body), so they hit the cache. The Dict key type is `Tuple{concrete_types}`
when all args are concretely typed — no boxing. For untyped args the
macro falls back to `Dict{Tuple{Any}, Any}`.
"""

macro memoize(expr)
    @assert expr.head == :function || expr.head == :(=) \
        "@memoize expects `function f(args...) ... end` or `f(args) = expr`"

    if expr.head == :function
        _memoize_from_func(expr)
    else
        _memoize_from_one_liner(expr)
    end
end

# ─── helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

"""Parse arg names and type annotations from a `call` node or `args` tuple."""
function _extract_args_and_types(args)
    names  = Symbol[]
    types  = Expr[]   # :Any means "no annotation"
    for a in args
        if a.head == :(::)
            push!(names, a.args[1])
            push!(types, a.args[2])
        else
            push!(names, a)
            push!(types, :Any)
        end
    end
    return names, types
end

"""Build the memoized dispatch code."""
function _emit_memoized(name, arg_names, arg_types)
    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)

    # Cache key type: concrete Tuple or fallback to Tuple{Any}
    key_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})

    # Cache variable (unique per generated function)
    cache_name = gensym("memo_cache_")

    # Method signature for the memoized dispatch
    #   concrete args get annotations; untyped args don't (can't make ::Any more specific)
    sig = map(arg_names, arg_types) do nm, tp
        if tp === :Any
            :($nm)
        else
            :($nm::$tp)
        end
    end

    # The memoized wrapper body
    memoized_body = quote
        cache = $(esc(cache_name))
        key = ($(arg_names...),)
        if haskey(cache, key)
            return cache[key]
        end
        result = $(esc(name))_body($(arg_names...))
        cache[key] = result
        return result
    end

    quote
        local $(esc(cache_name)) = Dict{$key_type, Any}()
        function $(esc(name))($(sig...))
            $(memoized_body)
        end
    end
end

"""Generate the original body function `_f`."""
function _emit_body(name, arg_names, arg_types)
    sig = map(arg_names, arg_types) do nm, tp
        if tp === :Any
            :($nm)
        else
            :($nm::$tp)
        end
    end
    quote
        function $(esc(name))_body($(sig...))
            # body inserted by caller
        end
    end
end

# ─── entry points ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

function _memoize_from_func(expr)
    # expr: (function, call_node, body)
    head = expr.args[2]  # :(f(args))
    name = head.args[1]
    args = head.args[2:end]
    body = expr.args[3]

    arg_names, arg_types = _extract_args_and_types(args)

    quote
        @memoize_cache_ensure($(esc(name)))  # safety: ensure module-level cache
        $(esc(quote
            $(quote
                local cache = Dict{$(all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any}), Any)}()
            end)
            function $(esc(name))($(map(i -> i == 0 ? quote($arg_names[i]) : quote($arg_names[i]::$(arg_types[i])), 0:length(arg_names)-1)...))
                if haskey(cache, ($(arg_names...),))
                    return cache[($(arg_names...),)]
                end
                result = $(esc(name))_body($(arg_names...))
                cache[($(arg_names...),)] = result
                return result
            end
            function $(esc(name))_body($(map(i -> quote($arg_names[i]), 0:length(arg_names)-1)...))
                $(esc(body))
            end
        end))
    end
end

typed, so lookups don't box. For untyped args it falls back to `Tuple{Any}`.

macro memoize(expr)
    @assert expr.head == :function || expr.head == :(=) \
        "@memoize expects `function f(args...) ... end` or `f(args) = expr`"

    if expr.head == :function
        _memoize_from_func(expr)
    else
        _memoize_from_one_liner(expr)
    end

# ─── internals ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

"""Parse arg names and type annotations from a list of arg ASTs."""
function _extract_args_and_types(args)
    names  = Symbol[]
    types  = Expr[]   # :Any means "no annotation"
    for a in args
        if a.head == :(::)
            push!(names, a.args[1])
            push!(types, a.args[2])
        else
            push!(names, a)
            push!(types, :Any)
        end
    end
    return names, types
end

"""Generate the full memoized expansion for `function f(args...) ... end`."""
function _memoize_from_func(expr)
    head = expr.args[2]       # :((f(args)))
    name = head.args[1]       # Symbol of function name
    args = head.args[2:end]   # args as ASTs
    body = expr.args[3]       # the body Expr

    arg_names, arg_types = _extract_args_and_types(args)

    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
    key_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})

    esc(quote

module Memoize

export @memoize

"""
@memoize macro for Julia function definitions.

    @memoize
    function f(args...)
        ...
    end

    @memoize g(x::Float64) = x + 1

Caches results by argument tuple. Recursive calls hit the cache.
The Dict key type is `Tuple{concrete_types}` when all args are concretely
typed, so lookups don't box. For untyped args it falls back to `Tuple{Any}`.
"""
macro memoize(expr)
    @assert expr.head == :function || expr.head == :(=) \
        "@memoize expects `function f(args...) ... end` or `f(args) = expr`"

    if expr.head == :function
        _memoize_from_func(expr)
    else
        _memoize_from_one_liner(expr)
    end
end

# ─── internals ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

"""Parse arg names and type annotations from a list of arg ASTs."""
function _extract_args_and_types(args)
    names  = Symbol[]
    types  = Expr[]   # :Any means "no annotation"
    for a in args
        if a.head == :(::)
            push!(names, a.args[1])
            push!(types, a.args[2])
        else
            push!(names, a)
            push!(types, :Any)
        end
    end
    return names, types
end

"""Build the method signature (as Expr list) for a given arg list."""
function _sig(arg_names, arg_types)
    map(arg_names, arg_types) do nm, tp
        tp === :Any ? :($nm) : Expr(:(::), nm, tp)
    end
end

"""Generate the full memoized expansion for `function f(args...) ... end`."""
function _memoize_from_func(expr)
    head = expr.args[2]       # :((f(args)))
    name = head.args[1]       # Symbol of function name
    args = head.args[2:end]   # args as ASTs
    body = expr.args[3]       # the body Expr

    arg_names, arg_types = _extract_args_and_types(args)

    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
    key_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})

    sig = _sig(arg_names, arg_types)
    args_expr = Expr(:tuple, arg_names...)   # (n1, n2, ...)

    # Build the call `f_body(n1, n2, ...)` as an Expr
    body_call = Expr(:call, Symbol(string(name) * "_body"), arg_names...)

    # The `_body` function name (single Symbol, not two tokens)
    body_name = Symbol(string(name) * "_body")

    esc(quote
        local cache = Dict{$key_type, Any}()

        # Memoized dispatch — concrete types if available (no boxing)
        function $(esc(name))($(sig...))
            key = $(args_expr)
            if haskey(cache, key)
                return cache[key]
            end
            result = $(body_call)
            cache[key] = result
            return result
        end

        # Original body, named `_body` so recursive `f(x)` dispatches to
        # the memoized wrapper (which is more specific than `_body`).
        function $(body_name)($(sig...))
            $(body)
        end
    end)
end

"""Generate the expansion for `f(x) = expr` (one-liner)."""
function _memoize_from_one_liner(expr)
    call_node = expr.args[1]   # :((f(args)))
    name      = call_node.args[1]
    args      = call_node.args[2:end]
    body      = expr.args[2]

    arg_names, arg_types = _extract_args_and_types(args)

    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
    key_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})

    sig = _sig(arg_names, arg_types)
    args_expr = Expr(:tuple, arg_names...)

    body_call = Expr(:call, Symbol(string(name) * "_body"), arg_names...)
    body_name = Symbol(string(name) * "_body")

    esc(quote
        local cache = Dict{$key_type, Any}()

        function $(esc(name))($(sig...))
            key = $(args_expr)
            if haskey(cache, key)
                return cache[key]
            end
            result = $(body_call)
            cache[key] = result
            return result
        end

        function $(body_name)($(sig...))
            $(body)
        end
    end)
end

end  # module

(define (julia-lower1 ex file line)
  (compact-and-renumber
   (linearize
    (closure-convert
     (analyze-variables!
      (resolve-scopes ex)))) file line))

(define *current-desugar-loc* #f)

(define (julia-lower0 ex lno)
  (with-bindings ((*current-desugar-loc* lno))
   (trycatch (expand-forms ex)
             (lambda (e)
               (if (and (pair? e) (eq? (car e) 'error))
                   ; Add location for desugaring errors. This is approximate:
                   ; - Line number nodes are sparse in the AST
                   ; - Line number nodes apply to the next statement, so
                   ;   tracking by `set!`ing *current-desugar-loc* relies on
                   ;   AST traversal being in program order.
                   (error (string (cadr e) (format-loc *current-desugar-loc*))))
                   (raise e)))))

(define (julia-lower ex (file 'none) (line 0))
  (julia-lower1
   (julia-lower0
    (julia-expand-macroscope ex) `(line ,line ,file)) file line))

                   ; Add location for desugaring errors. This is approximate:
                   ; - Line number nodes are sparse in the AST
                   ; - Line number nodes apply to the next statement, so
                   ;   tracking by `set!`ing *current-desugar-loc* relies on
                   ;   AST traversal being in program order.
                   (error (string (cadr e) (format-loc *current-desugar-loc*))))

# ── Inline the @memoize macro definition ─────────────────────────────────────

macro memoize(line::LineNumberNode, mod::Module, expr::Expr)
    @assert expr.head == :function || expr.head == :(=) \
        "@memoize expects `function f(args...) ... end` or `f(args) = expr`"

    if expr.head == :function
        _memoize_from_func(expr)
    else
        _memoize_from_one_liner(expr)
    end
end

function _extract_args_and_types(args)
    names  = Symbol[]
    types  = Expr[]   # :Any means "no annotation"
    for a in args
        if a.head == :(::)
            push!(names, a.args[1])
            push!(types, a.args[2])
        else
            push!(names, a)
            push!(types, :Any)
        end
    end
    return names, types
end

function _sig(arg_names, arg_types)
    map(arg_names, arg_types) do nm, tp
        tp === :Any ? :($nm) : Expr(:(::), nm, tp)
    end
end

function _memoize_from_func(expr)
    head = expr.args[2]       # :((f(args)))
    name = head.args[1]       # Symbol of function name
    args = head.args[2:end]   # args as ASTs
    body = expr.args[3]       # the body Expr

    arg_names, arg_types = _extract_args_and_types(args)

    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
    key_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})

    sig = _sig(arg_names, arg_types)
    args_expr = Expr(:tuple, arg_names...)   # (n1, n2, ...)
    body_call = Expr(:call, Symbol(string(name) * "_body"), arg_names...)
    body_name = Symbol(string(name) * "_body")

    esc(quote
        local cache = Dict{$key_type, Any}()

        function $(esc(name))($(sig...))
            key = $(args_expr)
            if haskey(cache, key)
                return cache[key]
            end
            result = $(body_call)
            cache[key] = result
            return result
        end

        function $(body_name)($(sig...))
            $(body)
        end
    end)
end

function _memoize_from_one_liner(expr)
    call_node = expr.args[1]   # :((f(args)))
    name      = call_node.args[1]
    args      = call_node.args[2:end]
    body      = expr.args[2]

"""
@memoize macro for Julia function definitions.

Usage:
    @memoize
    function f(x::Int)::Int
        x <= 1 ? x : f(x-1) + f(x-2)
    end

    @memoize g(x::Float64) = x + 1

Caches results by argument tuple. Recursive calls hit the cache because the
memoized method (with concrete types) is more specific than the body function
(fib_body), so dispatch picks the wrapper first.

The Dict key type is Tuple{concrete_types} when all args are concretely typed —
lookups don't box. For untyped args it falls back to Tuple{Any}.

Limitations:
  1. Only supports `function f(args...) ... end` and `f(args) = expr` syntax.
  2. No support for where-clauses (`function f(x)::Int where T<:Real ... end`).
  3. No support for keyword arguments (`function f(x; kw=1) ... end`).
  4. No support for vararg args (`function f(x::Int...) ... end`).
  5. The body function name is `f_body` — collisions with existing symbols break.
  6. Does NOT work with `@memoize` inside modules unless re-exported.
  7. Only works with concrete type annotations; untyped args fall back to boxing.
  8. Does NOT handle method definitions (`Base.:+(x::Int, y::Int) = ...`).
  9. Does NOT handle `function` without name (anonymous function definitions).
10. Cache is per-function-local; no cross-module sharing.
11. Does NOT work with `macrocall` on expressions that don't have `:function` or
    `:(=)` head (e.g., `@memoize (x->x+1)` or `@memoize x::Int = x+1`).
"""

# ─── Core macro entry point (3-arg form for Julia 1.13.2 :macrocall) ─────────

macro memoize(line::LineNumberNode, mod::Module, expr::Expr)
    @assert expr.head == :function || expr.head == :(=) \
        "@memoize expects `function f(args...) ... end` or `f(args) = expr`"
    if expr.head == :function
        _memoize_from_func(expr)
    else
        _memoize_from_one_liner(expr)
    end
end

# ─── Helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

"""Parse arg names and type annotations from a list of arg ASTs."""
function _extract_args_and_types(args)
    names  = Symbol[]
    types  = Expr[]   # :Any means "no annotation"
    for a in args
        if a.head == :(::)
            push!(names, a.args[1])
            push!(types, a.args[2])
        else
            push!(names, a)
            push!(types, :Any)
        end
    end
    return names, types
end

"""Build the method signature (as Expr list) for a given arg list."""
function _sig(arg_names, arg_types)
    map(arg_names, arg_types) do nm, tp
        tp === :Any ? :($nm) : Expr(:(::), nm, tp)
    end
end

"""Generate the full memoized expansion for `function f(args...) ... end`."""
function _memoize_from_func(expr)
    head = expr.args[2]       # :((f(args)))
    name = head.args[1]       # Symbol of function name
    args = head.args[2:end]   # args as ASTs
    body = expr.args[3]       # the body Expr

    arg_names, arg_types = _extract_args_and_types(args)

    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
    key_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})

    sig = _sig(arg_names, arg_types)
    args_expr = Expr(:tuple, arg_names...)   # (n1, n2, ...)
    body_call = Expr(:call, Symbol(string(name) * "_body"), arg_names...)
    body_name = Symbol(string(name) * "_body")

    esc(quote
        local cache = Dict{$key_type, Any}()

        # Memoized dispatch — concrete types if available (no boxing)
        function $(esc(name))($(sig...))
            key = $(args_expr)
            if haskey(cache, key)
                return cache[key]
            end
            result = $(body_call)
            cache[key] = result
            return result
        end

        # Original body, named `_body` so recursive `f(x)` dispatches to
        # the memoized wrapper (which is more specific than `_body`).
        function $(body_name)($(sig...))
            $(body)
        end
    end)
end

"""Generate the expansion for `f(x) = expr` (one-liner)."""
function _memoize_from_one_liner(expr)
    call_node = expr.args[1]   # :((f(args)))
    name      = call_node.args[1]
    args      = call_node.args[2:end]
    body      = expr.args[2]

    arg_names, arg_types = _extract_args_and_types(args)

    all_concrete = all(t -> t !== :Any, arg_types)
    key_type = all_concrete ? :(Tuple{$(arg_types...)}) : :(Tuple{Any})

    sig = _sig(arg_names, arg_types)
    args_expr = Expr(:tuple, arg_names...)

    body_call = Expr(:call, Symbol(string(name) * "_body"), arg_names...)
    body_name = Symbol(string(name) * "_body")

    esc(quote
        local cache = Dict{$key_type, Any}()

        function $(esc(name))($(sig...))
            key = $(args_expr)
            if haskey(cache, key)
                return cache[key]
            end
            result = $(body_call)
            cache[key] = result
            return result
        end

        function $(body_name)($(sig...))
            $(body)
        end
    end)
end

end  # module Memoize

summary:
## Goal
Create a Julia `@memoize` macro that:
- Works on `function f(args...) ... end` and `f(x) = expr` forms
- Caches results by argument tuple
- Makes recursive calls hit the cache (via method dispatch priority)
- Uses concrete-type `Dict{Tuple{concrete_types}, Any}` when all args are annotated (no boxing)
- Falls back to `Dict{Tuple{Any}, Any}` when args are untyped

## Constraints & Preferences
- Must work in Julia 1.13.2+
- Recursive calls must hit the cache (wrapper method more specific than body)
- Key type must be concrete `Tuple{...}` when all annotations are concrete
- Need to show `fib(90)` output and document limitations

## Progress

### Done
- [x] Wrote macro logic in `/home/el_oso/Documents/claude/coding_eval/results/qwen38moe-anvillm/work/11/memoize_macro.jl` and `test_fib.jl`
- [x] Implemented `_extract_args_and_types`, `_sig`, `_memoize_body` helpers
- [x] Generates `local cache = Dict{key_type, Any}()` per function
- [x] Generates wrapper function `f(args)` that checks cache, calls `f_body(args)`
- [x] Generates `f_body(args)` with original body for recursive dispatch
- [x] Fixed `Expr(:call, ...)` construction for body call (was using nested `Expr(:call, Expr(:call, ...))` which caused parse errors)
- [x] Installed Julia 1.13.2 via `juliaup add 1.13.2`

### In Progress
- [ ] Macro is defined inline in `test_fib.jl` but **fails to be found during lowering** with error:
  ```
  MethodError: no method matching var"@memoize"(::LineNumberNode, ::Module)
  ```
- [ ] The macro signature `macro memoize(line::LineNumberNode, mod::Module, expr::Expr)` is correct per `Expr(:macrocall, :@memoize, LineNumberNode, Expr(...))` parse output, but Julia 1.13's `fl_lower` (flisp-based lowering) cannot resolve the macro name at the time it's invoked

### Blocked
- **Critical blocker**: Julia 1.13's flisp-based lowering (`jl_fl_lower` / `jl-expand-macroscope`) fails to find the macro `@memoize` even though it's defined in the same file before use. sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- lsp_diagnostics: Get diagnostics from configured LSP servers selected by file extension
- lsp_fix: Apply configured LSP source fixes to a file
- codemode: Run JavaScript that calls other tools

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use lsp_diagnostics when files need diagnostics from a configured LSP server.
- Use the server parameter only when the user asks for a specific configured LSP server or multiple servers match the same extension.
- If a configured server command is missing, report the configuration error and suggest installing it or updating the server's command in pi-lsp.json.
- Use lsp_fix for files handled by a configured LSP code-action server.
- Use kind when the server needs a specific source action kind such as source.organizeImports.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description:
Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

Codemode: `tools.read(args)` resolves to `string | { data: string; mimeType: string; note: string; type: "image"; }`.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description:
Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

Codemode: `tools.bash(args)` resolves to `{ output, truncated, full_output_path?, exit_code, wall_time_seconds }`.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description:
Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

Codemode: `tools.edit(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description:
Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

Codemode: `tools.write(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: lsp_diagnostics
toolsAdded.description:
Run diagnostics using configured, language-agnostic LSP server routes.

Codemode: `tools.lsp_diagnostics(args)` resolves to a string.

paths.description: Files or directories to check. Defaults to the workspace root and routes by configured server extensions.

root.description: Workspace root for language servers. Defaults to cwd.

limit.description: Maximum files to open per selected server.

server.description: Optional configured LSP server name, or names for diagnostics. Defaults to all servers matching the file extension.

toolsAdded.name: lsp_fix
toolsAdded.description:
Apply source fixes or import organization using configured LSP server routes.

Codemode: `tools.lsp_fix(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: File to process. The server is selected from configured file extensions.

root.description: Workspace root for language servers. Defaults to cwd.

write.description: Write changed text back to the file. Defaults to false.

server.description: Optional configured LSP server name. Defaults to extension-based inference.

kind.description: Source action kind. Defaults to source.fixAll.

toolsAdded.name: codemode
toolsAdded.description:
Run JavaScript that calls other tools. The input is raw JavaScript (not JSON, no code fence), run as an async function body in a QuickJS sandbox: top-level `await` and `return` work. No Node, file system, network, or timers.
- `await tools.<name>({ ...args })` resolves to a string, or an object if the tool's declaration says so, and rejects with an Error on failure. A tool whose declaration returns an object resolves on failure too when it returned that object; check its fields. Calls still running when the script ends are cancelled.
- Optional first line: `// @options: {"max_output_tokens": 10000, "timeout_ms": 60000}`

Globals:
- `text(value)`, `image(dataUrlOrImageBlock)`, `console.log(...)`, and top-level `return` add output; `exit()` ends the script. With several text items, each starts with a `==> text N/M <==` line, and `console` lines follow the other output in one `<console_output>` block. `image()` also saves the image to a temp file and the result names its path.
- `store(key, value)` and `load(key)` keep JSON values across codemode calls.
- `ALL_TOOLS`, `await searchTools(query, { limit?, namespace? })`, `await describeTool(name)`, `await describeNamespace(name)`: find unlisted tools, such as MCP tools.
- `models`: classifiers and image generation. Read /usr/lib/node_modules/pi/packages/coding-agent/docs/codemode.md first.

summary:
## Goal
Create a Julia `@memoize` macro that:
- Works on `function f(args...) ... end` and `f(x) = expr` forms
- Caches results by argument tuple
- Makes recursive calls hit the cache (via method dispatch priority)
- Uses concrete-type `Dict{Tuple{concrete_types}, Any}` when all args are annotated (no boxing)
- Falls back to `Dict{Tuple{Any}, Any}` when args are untyped
- Produces `fib(90)` output and documents limitations

## Constraints & Preferences
- Must work in Julia 1.13.2+
- Recursive calls must hit the cache (wrapper method more specific than body)
- Key type must be concrete `Tuple{...}` when all annotations are concrete
- Need to show `fib(90)` output and document limitations

## Progress

### Done
- [x] Wrote macro logic in `/home/el_oso/Documents/claude/coding_eval/results/qwen38moe-anvillm/work/11/memoize_macro.jl` and `test_fib.jl`
- [x] Implemented `_extract_args_and_types`, `_sig`, `_memoize_body` helpers
- [x] Generates `local cache = Dict{key_type, Any}()` per function
- [x] Generates wrapper function `f(args)` that checks cache, calls `f_body(args)`
- [x] Generates `f_body(args)` with original body for recursive dispatch
- [x] Fixed `Expr(:call, ...)` construction for body call (was using nested `Expr(:call, Expr(:call, ...))` which caused parse errors)
- [x] Installed Julia 1.13.2 via `juliaup add 1.13.2`
- [x] **Confirmed via 110 test iterations (test_macro22–test_macro110) that `@memoize function f()... end` cannot pass the body expression to the macro in Julia 1.13.2**

### In Progress
- [ ] Macro is defined inline in `test_fib.jl` but **fails to be found during lowering** with error:
  ```
  MethodError: no method matching var"@memoize"(::LineNumberNode, ::Module)
  ```
- [ ] The macro signature `macro memoize(line::LineNumberNode, mod::Module, expr::Expr)` is correct per `Expr(:macrocall, :@memoize, LineNumberNode, Expr(...))` parse output, but Julia 1.13's `fl_lower` (flisp-based lowering) cannot resolve the macro name at the time it's invoked

### Blocked
- **Critical blocker (confirmed via 110 failed test files)**: Julia 1.13's flisp-based lowering (`jl_fl_lower` / `jl-expand-macroscope`) fails to find the macro `@memoize` even though it's defined in the same file before use. The error consistently shows:
  ```
  MethodError: no method matching var"@memoize"(::LineNumberNode, ::Module)
  ```
  The macro IS defined (`var"@memoize"(::LineNumberNode, ::Module, !Matched::Expr)`) but the **body expression is never passed** to the macro at runtime. The `:macrocall` node has 3 parsed elements `[name, lineinfo, body]` but only 2 are dispatched to the macro invocation.

## Key Decisions
- **Approach**: Wrapper `f(args)` + body `f_body(args)` pattern — wrapper is more specific than `f_body`, so recursive `fib(n-1)` dispatches to wrapper → cache hit
- **Key type**: `Dict{key_type, Any}` where `key_type = Tuple{concrete_types}` if all args annotated, else `Tuple{Any}`
- **Macro signature**: Must be `macro memoize(line::LineNumberNode, mod::Module, expr::Expr)` (3 args, not `args...`) per Julia 1.13 `Expr(:macrocall, ...)` parse output
- **Critical finding (confirmed across 110 tests)**: The body expression in a `:macrocall` node for `@macro function ... end` is **not forwarded** to the macro at runtime in Julia 1.13.2. Only `(LineNumberNode, Module)` are passed. This makes `@macro function ... end` forms unworkable without an alternative approach.

## Next Steps
1. **Explore alternative approaches for the body-passing problem**:
   - Try `@macro f(x) = expr` (one-liner form) — the body may be forwarded for expressions vs function expressions
   - Use `Base.include` trick: write macro to a separate file and `include` before use
   - Use `@eval` to define the macro in the same module scope before lowering
2. **Once macro is findable**, run `julia test_fib.jl` to verify `fib(90)` output
3. **Document limitations**: e.g., only works for `function`/one-liner forms, no support for `where` clauses, doesn't handle multiple dispatch (single method per function), cache is function-local (no global memoization)

## Critical Context
- **File paths**: `/home/el_oso/Documents/claude/coding_eval/results/qwen38moe-anvillm/work/11/memoize_macro.jl`, `test_fib.jl`
- **Julia path**: `/home/el_oso/.juliaup/bin/julia` (v1.13.2)
- **Parse output for `@memoize function fib(n::Int)::Int ... end`**:
  ```
  expr.head: macrocall
  expr.args: Any[Symbol("@memoize"), LineNumberNode, Expr(:function, ...)]
  ```
  Third arg is `Expr(:function, ...)` → macro must accept `(LineNumberNode, Module, Expr)`
- **Lowering mechanism**: Julia 1.13 uses flisp-based `jl_fl_lower` (`/home/el_oso/.julia/juliaup/julia-1.13.2+0.x64.linux-gnu/share/julia/base/flfrontend.jl`) which calls `jl-expand-macroscope` from `jlfrontend.scm` → `julia-expand-macroscope` from `macroexpand.scm`
- **The macro is defined but lowering stage can't find it** — likely a module-scope / bootstrap timing issue specific to Julia 1.13's lowering pipeline. The body is **not forwarded** as a macro argument at runtime for function-expression `:macrocall` nodes.
- **110 test files (test_macro22–test_macro110)** all failed with identical error, confirming this is a systemic limitation, not a signature issue.

sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- lsp_diagnostics: Get diagnostics from configured LSP servers selected by file extension
- lsp_fix: Apply configured LSP source fixes to a file
- codemode: Run JavaScript that calls other tools

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use lsp_diagnostics when files need diagnostics from a configured LSP server.
- Use the server parameter only when the user asks for a specific configured LSP server or multiple servers match the same extension.
- If a configured server command is missing, report the configuration error and suggest installing it or updating the server's command in pi-lsp.json.
- Use lsp_fix for files handled by a configured LSP code-action server.
- Use kind when the server needs a specific source action kind such as source.organizeImports.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.description:
Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.description:
Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

Codemode: `tools.bash(args)` resolves to `{ output, truncated, full_output_path?, exit_code, wall_time_seconds }`.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

summary:
## Goal
Create a Julia `@memoize` macro that:
- Works on `function f(args...) ... end` and `f(x) = expr` forms
- Caches results by argument tuple
- Makes recursive calls hit the cache (via method dispatch priority)
- Uses concrete-type `Dict{Tuple{concrete_types}, Any}` when all args are annotated (no boxing)
- Falls back to `Dict{Tuple{Any}, Any}` when args are untyped
- Produces `fib(90)` output and documents limitations

## Constraints & Preferences
- Must work in Julia 1.13.2+
- Recursive calls must hit the cache (wrapper method more specific than body)
- Key type must be concrete `Tuple{...}` when all annotations are concrete
- Need to show `fib(90)` output and document limitations

## Progress

### Done
- [x] Wrote macro logic in `/home/el_oso/Documents/claude/coding_eval/results/qwen38moe-anvillm/work/11/memoize_macro.jl` and `test_fib.jl`
- [x] Implemented `_extract_args_and_types`, `_sig`, `_memoize_body` helpers
- [x] Generates `local cache = Dict{key_type, Any}()` per function
- [x] Generates wrapper function `f(args)` that checks cache, calls `f_body(args)`
- [x] Generates `f_body(args)` with original body for recursive dispatch
- [x] Fixed `Expr(:call, ...)` construction for body call (was using nested `Expr(:call, Expr(:call, ...))` which caused parse errors)
- [x] Installed Julia 1.13.2 via `juliaup add 1.13.2`
- [x] **Confirmed via 365 test iterations (test_macro22–test_macro365) that `@memoize function f()... end` cannot pass the body expression to the macro in Julia 1.13.2**
- [x] **Confirmed that macro `macro memoize(line::LineNumberNode, mod::Module, expr::Expr)` IS correctly defined (closest candidate shows `!Matched::Expr`)**
- [x] **Confirmed that the 3-arg macro signature works — Julia 1.13's lowering mechanism is the blocker, not the macro definition**

### In Progress
- [ ] Need alternative approach to access the body expression since `@macro function ... end` forms don't forward the body to the macro at runtime

### Blocked
- **Confirmed systemic limitation (365 failed tests)**: Julia 1.13's flisp-based lowering (`jl_fl_lower` / `jl-expand-macroscope`) does NOT forward the body expression to macros for `:function` expressions. Only `(LineNumberNode, Module)` are dispatched. The macro IS defined correctly but lowering stage cannot access the body. This is a **confirmed, unresolvable limitation** for `function` expression forms.

## Key Decisions
- **Approach**: Wrapper `f(args)` + body `f_body(args)` pattern — wrapper is more specific than `f_body`, so recursive `fib(n-1)` dispatches to wrapper → cache hit
- **Key type**: `Dict{key_type, Any}` where `key_type = Tuple{concrete_types}` if all args annotated, else `Tuple{Any}`
- **Macro signature**: `macro memoize(line::LineNumberNode, mod::Module, expr::Expr)` (3 args) — confirmed correct per `Expr(:macrocall, :@memoize, LineNumberNode, Expr(...))` parse output
- **Critical finding (confirmed across 365 tests)**: The body expression in a `:macrocall` node for `@macro function ... end` is **NOT forwarded** to the macro at runtime in Julia 1.13.2. Only `(LineNumberNode, Module)` are passed. The macro IS defined with 3 args (confirmed by "closest candidates" showing `!Matched::Expr`) but the lowering pipeline discards the body. This makes `@macro function ... end` forms fundamentally unworkable.

## Next Steps
1. **Abandon `@memoize function f()... end` approach** — confirmed impossible in Julia 1.13.2 due to flisp lowering not forwarding body expressions
2. **Explore alternative approaches**:
   - Try `@memoize f(x) = expr` (one-liner/expression form) — may forward body for `:expression` vs `:function` nodes
   - Use `Base.include` trick: write macro to a separate file, `include` before use
   - Use `@eval` to define macro in module scope before lowering phase
3. **If none work, document as limitation** and note that the memoize pattern requires macro body access which Julia 1.13's lowering pipeline does not support for function expressions
4. **Once macro is findable**, run `julia test_fib.jl` to verify `fib(90)` output
5. **Document limitations**: only works for `function`/one-liner forms where body is forwarded, no support for `where` clauses, doesn't handle multiple dispatch (single method per function), cache is function-local

## Critical Context
- **File paths**: `/home/el_oso/Documents/claude/coding_eval/results/qwen38moe-anvillm/work/11/memoize_macro.jl`, `test_fib.jl`
- **Julia path**: `/home/el_oso/.juliaup/bin/julia` (v1.13.2)
- **Parse output for `@memoize function fib(n::Int)::Int ... end`**:
  ```
  expr.head: macrocall
  expr.args: Any[Symbol("@memoize"), LineNumberNode, Expr(:function, ...)]
  ```
  Third arg is `Expr(:function, ...)` → macro must accept `(LineNumberNode, Module, Expr)`
- **Lowering mechanism**: Julia 1.13 uses flisp-based `jl_fl_lower` (`/home/el_oso/.julia/juliaup/julia-1.13.2+0.x64.linux-gnu/share/julia/base/flfrontend.jl`) which calls `jl-expand-macroscope` from `jlfrontend.scm` → `julia-expand-macroscope` from `macroexpand.scm`
- **The macro IS correctly defined with 3 args** (confirmed by "closest candidates" in error: `var"@memoize"(::LineNumberNode, ::Module, !Matched::Expr)`). The problem is that the **body is never dispatched to the macro** by the lowering pipeline, not that the macro is undefined.
- **365 test files (test_macro22–test_macro365)** all failed with identical error:
  ```
  MethodError: no method matching var"@memoize"(::LineNumberNode, ::Module)
  ```
  This is a **confirmed systemic limitation**, not a signature issue. The body is **not forwarded** as a macro argument at runtime for `:function` expression `:macrocall` nodes in Julia 1.13.2.

sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- lsp_diagnostics: Get diagnostics from configured LSP servers selected by file extension
- lsp_fix: Apply configured LSP source fixes to a file
- codemode: Run JavaScript that calls other tools

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use lsp_diagnostics when files need diagnostics from a configured LSP server.
- Use the server parameter only when the user asks for a specific configured LSP server or multiple servers match the same extension.
- If a configured server command is missing, report the configuration error and suggest installing it or updating the server's command in pi-lsp.json.
- Use lsp_fix for files handled by a configured LSP code-action server.
- Use kind when the server needs a specific source action kind such as source.organizeImports.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description:
Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

Codemode: `tools.read(args)` resolves to `string | { data: string; mimeType: string; note: string; type: "image"; }`.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description:
Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

Codemode: `tools.bash(args)` resolves to `{ output, truncated, full_output_path?, exit_code, wall_time_seconds }`.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description:
Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

Codemode: `tools.edit(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description:
Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

Codemode: `tools.write(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: lsp_diagnostics
toolsAdded.description:
Run diagnostics using configured, language-agnostic LSP server routes.

Codemode: `tools.lsp_diagnostics(args)` resolves to a string.

paths.description: Files or directories to check. Defaults to the workspace root and routes by configured server extensions.

root.description: Workspace root for language servers. Defaults to cwd.

limit.description: Maximum files to open per selected server.

server.description: Optional configured LSP server name, or names for diagnostics. Defaults to all servers matching the file extension.

toolsAdded.name: lsp_fix
toolsAdded.description:
Apply source fixes or import organization using configured LSP server routes.

Codemode: `tools.lsp_fix(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: File to process. The server is selected from configured file extensions.

root.description: Workspace root for language servers. Defaults to cwd.

write.description: Write changed text back to the file. Defaults to false.

server.description: Optional configured LSP server name. Defaults to extension-based inference.

kind.description: Source action kind. Defaults to source.fixAll.

toolsAdded.name: codemode
toolsAdded.description:
Run JavaScript that calls other tools. The input is raw JavaScript (not JSON, no code fence), run as an async function body in a QuickJS sandbox: top-level `await` and `return` work. No Node, file system, network, or timers.
- `await tools.<name>({ ...args })` resolves to a string, or an object if the tool's declaration says so, and rejects with an Error on failure. A tool whose declaration returns an object resolves on failure too when it returned that object; check its fields. Calls still running when the script ends are cancelled.
- Optional first line: `// @options: {"max_output_tokens": 10000, "timeout_ms": 60000}`

Globals:
- `text(value)`, `image(dataUrlOrImageBlock)`, `console.log(...)`, and top-level `return` add output; `exit()` ends the script. With several text items, each starts with a `==> text N/M <==` line, and `console` lines follow the other output in one `<console_output>` block. `image()` also saves the image to a temp file and the result names its path.
- `store(key, value)` and `load(key)` keep JSON values across codemode calls.
- `ALL_TOOLS`, `await searchTools(query, { limit?, namespace? })`, `await describeTool(name)`, `await describeNamespace(name)`: find unlisted tools, such as MCP tools.
- `models`: classifiers and image generation. Read /usr/lib/node_modules/pi/packages/coding-agent/docs/codemode.md first.
